newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin and Chirac to discuss NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin and Chirac to discuss NATO expansion.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin was due to meet French President Jacques Chirac on Sunday, taking the world stage for the first time since a bout of pneumonia which has raised questions over his ability to rule Russia.

Yeltsin was expected to take a tough line on NATO plans for eastward expansion when he met Chirac at a country residence near Moscow. But much world and domestic attention will be focused on his health rather than his words.

Yeltsin's few appearances on television since his release from hospital on January 20 have shown him looking aged and rather frail. He has yet to undergo the scrutiny which will accompany a meeting with a foreign leader.

The Russian president spent Saturday, his 66th birthday, quietly with his family. He was joined in the evening by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, just back from an economic summit in Switzerland, and chief aide Anatoly Chubais.
Yeltsin's wife, Naina, said the president, who had a heart bypass operation in November, was recovering well.

"Doctors say that if it were just a normal man he should have stayed in hospital...It takes longer to recover if you work at the same time." His condition, she said, allowed him more time to watch television and to think.
"Now he has more time to...weigh things," she said in a television interview. His daughter, Tatyana, said the family had bought the president a quilted jacket as a present.
Chirac, along with other Western leaders, sees Yeltsin's survival as essential to economic reform in Russia.

Interfax quoted government experts as saying that the two leaders would discuss prospects of promoting stronger bilateral trade and economic links and creating a better climate for French investment in Russia.
But the talks would focus on NATO's plans to begin talks later this year to incorporate some of Moscow's former Warsaw Pact allies, including Poland. Russia sees in this a threat to its security.

But since NATO made clear that Russia's objections would not stop its expansion, Moscow appears to have switched to negotiating a deal which would keep the alliance's military structures away from its borders.
Government officials say Russia is seeking a binding document rather than a political declaration.
They say that in an ideal world this document should include a promise not to deploy nuclear forces, heavy weapons and troops belonging to other NATO states on the territory of new members.
Moscow is clearly looking for support from within NATO, especially from some of its European members who seek to take over some alliance command functions from the United States.
Government officials have said that Moscow closely watched debates between Washington and Paris about whether an American or European should command NATO's southern flank.

A French official has said that Paris supported Moscow's demands for a binding charter on Russia-NATO relations and felt the United States was still trying to fob off the Russians with a few, non-binding pledges.
Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.
Chirac hopes NATO can work out a deal with Russia before an alliance summit in Madrid in July at which it is expected to issue invitations to some eastern European states.
